nodes.text: Example: A steady current of 2.5 A is created in a wire for 1.0 minute. How much charge passed by any given point, and how many electrons would this be?

nodes.spoken_math_alternative: I equals Q divided by delta t, which leads to I equals 2.5 coulombs per second, equal to Q divided by t.
Q equals I times t, equal to 2.5 coulombs per second times 60 seconds, equal to 150 coulombs.
N equals 150 coulombs times one electron per 1.6 times 10 to the negative 19 coulombs, equal to 9.4 times 10 to the 20 electrons.
n equals 9.4 times 10 to the 20 electrons times one divided by 6.022 times 10 to the 23 electrons per mole, equal to 0.0016 mole.

nodes.detailed_figure_description: A closed rectangular circuit contains a battery on the left and a zigzag resistor on the right. The battery is labeled V, with its upper terminal marked positive and its lower terminal marked negative. The resistor is labeled R. Multiple arrows labeled e⁻ show electron flow counterclockwise: rightward along the bottom wire, upward through the resistor side, leftward along the top wire, and downward along the battery side.
nodes.figure_alternative: Battery-and-resistor circuit showing counterclockwise electron flow.
The circuit symbol for a resistor: R followed by a horizontal wire with a zigzag section. An arrow labels it “circuit symbol.”

nodes.spoken_math_alternative: The units of ohms equal volts per ampere, equal joules per coulomb divided by coulombs per second.

nodes.text: A resistor resists the flow of current. They’re often used to limit current in a part of a circuit. Wires themselves have some resistance, but we’ll usually ignore it.
